narrative_idea_gen: Presented as a compiled dossier of video diaries, text chains, and increasingly unhinged peer-review comments, *The Gundersen Protocol* follows Dr. Mara Shin—a disgraced veterinary dentist turned science journalist—as she assembles a team of seven spectacularly overqualified medical specialists to investigate an abandoned fertility clinic in rural Saskatchewan where, according to local legend, a rogue endocrinologist successfully gestated a human baby inside a pumpkin in 2011. Each expert privately believes the expedition is career suicide and the pumpkin-baby story is obvious nonsense, but every one of them assumes the others are genuinely enthusiastic, so they keep escalating their commitment—funding travel, signing liability waivers, purchasing hazmat gear—until they're standing in the derelict clinic staring at rows of soil-filled incubators and a functioning grow light that nobody can explain. The documentary layers are the joke and the hook: Mara's omniscient narration cheerfully reveals each team member's secret dread even as their on-camera interviews project breezy confidence, and the found footage slowly, hilariously shifts from debunking mission to the dawning, impossible realization that the pumpkins are *warm*.

# Seven Structural Beats for *The Gundersen Protocol*

---

## Beat 1: Mara Shin's Recruitment Pitch — The Legend Delivered in the Wrong Emotional Register

**Concrete Action:** Through a compiled layer of Mara's video diary and her outgoing emails/texts, establish the pumpkin-baby legend and Mara's campaign to assemble a team. Mara, disgraced and financially desperate, frames the expedition as a serious investigative documentary opportunity. Each specialist receives her pitch. Each privately thinks it is absurd. Each says yes — for reasons that have nothing to do with believing the story (career stagnation, divorce escape, grant money laundering, morbid curiosity, a crush on another team member). Mara's narration cheerfully discloses every private motive the camera never captures.

**Structural Function — Plant the Central Threat Inside a Dismissal Framework:** This beat must accomplish exactly what O'Connor does with the Misfit's newspaper clipping: introduce the story's core supernatural element (a baby gestated inside a pumpkin) in a context so transparently ridiculous that the audience files it away as *the joke* rather than *the point*. The pumpkin story should be presented through layers of ironic distance — local legend, tabloid clipping, Mara's half-embarrassed pitch — so the reader bonds with the debunkers. Every specialist's private skepticism should mirror the reader's own, creating a conspiracy of condescension. The audience must be *taught to laugh at the premise* so that the premise's eventual validation lands as a betrayal of the tonal contract.

**Key Craft Problem to Solve:** The dossier format must be established here as both the story's formal gimmick and its deepest structural tool. The gap between what people say on camera and what Mara's narration reveals they actually think is not just comedy — it is the engine of dramatic irony that will power the entire middle act. Every document type (video diary, text chain, peer-review comment, email) should be introduced in this beat so the reader learns to read the format fluently before the format starts being used against them.

**What Must Land:** The reader should leave this beat confident they are reading a satire about academic careerism and groupthink. They should find the pumpkin story funny. They should feel smarter than the characters. This superiority is the trap.

---

## Beat 2: The Abilene Spiral — Escalating Commitment Through Mutual Misreading

**Concrete Action:** Through intercut text chains, group emails, and individual video diaries, show the team's preparation escalating far beyond what any single member intended. Someone books flights. Someone else responds by purchasing hazmat gear, which causes a third person to sign a liability waiver, which causes Mara to lease an equipment van. Each escalation is interpreted by the others as evidence of genuine enthusiasm, which pressures the next person to match it. Mara's narration maps the precise causal chain of social coercion, naming each misreading in real time. Private text threads between individual members reveal mounting panic: *"Do you actually think this is real?" "I assumed YOU thought it was real." "I only signed up because Dr. Kovacs signed up." "Kovacs told me he only signed up because of YOU."*

**Structural Function — Build the Causal Machine from Character Flaws:** This is the equivalent of O'Connor's car ride: a seemingly episodic, comedic sequence in which every detail is secretly load-bearing. Each specialist's particular brand of professional vanity, social anxiety, or emotional need must be established as a *specific comic trait* that is simultaneously the mechanism driving them toward Saskatchewan. The hidden cat in O'Connor's story is the grandmother's concealed selfishness; here, the hidden cat is *collective self-deception* — no one will be the first to admit they think the mission is absurd because admitting it means admitting they joined for embarrassing personal reasons.

**Key Craft Problem to Solve:** Seven specialists plus Mara is a large cast. This beat must differentiate them efficiently through their document voices — the way each person texts, the register of their video diaries, their peer-review commenting style. Not all seven need equal weight. Identify three or four who will carry the thematic load and give them the most distinctive document signatures. The others can function as a chorus. The format itself should do the characterization work: a person is revealed by whether they write formal emails or chaotic texts, whether their video diaries are rehearsed or raw.

**What Must Land:** The comedy of the Abilene Paradox should be genuinely, structurally funny — not just described as funny but *enacted* through the document layering so the reader watches the misunderstandings cascade in real time. But underneath the comedy, a precise causal chain must be legible: these specific people, with these specific insecurities, could not have done anything other than end up on this road. The comedy is the machinery. The machinery is aimed at the clinic.

---

## Beat 3: The Last Night Before the Clinic — The Consensus of False Skepticism

**Concrete Action:** The team arrives in rural Saskatchewan and gathers at a motel or bar the night before entering the clinic. On camera, they perform collegial skepticism — trading jokes about the pumpkin baby, one-upping each other with debunking hypotheses, bonding over their shared rationalism. This is their Red Sammy's scene: a group of people agreeing on a comfortable consensus that flatters their self-image. Mara's narration, or intercut private video diaries recorded in motel rooms afterward, reveals the first cracks — small, inadmissible feelings. Someone Googled the rogue endocrinologist (Dr. Gundersen?) and found his publication history unsettlingly legitimate. Someone noticed the locals don't laugh when the pumpkin story comes up. Someone can't sleep.

**Structural Function — Define the Thematic Term Through Ironic Consensus, Then Begin Undermining It:** O'Connor's Red Sammy scene defines "good" as a bankrupt social performance. This beat must define "rational" or "scientific" as the equivalent bankrupt performance. The team's aggressive skepticism should feel, to the reader, exactly as hollow as the grandmother's morality — not because skepticism is wrong, but because *their* skepticism is social rather than genuine. They are performing disbelief for each other the same way the grandmother performs virtue. The phrase equivalent to "a good man is hard to find" might be some version of a team member's confident debunking line that the reader will remember with horror later — a claim about what is and isn't biologically possible that the clinic will quietly, horribly disprove.

**Key Craft Problem to Solve:** This is the hinge beat — the last moment of normalcy, the last meal. It must be warm enough that the reader enjoys these people's company. If the team is only pompous, the turn to horror won't hurt. At least two or three members need to be genuinely likable in their vulnerability here. A private video diary where someone admits they *wanted* the story to be true — that they came because their life is so depleted of wonder that even a debunking mission felt like an adventure — would give the reader an emotional anchor for everything that follows. The comedy must have a tender underbelly, or the horror has nothing soft to bite into.

**What Must Land:** The reader should feel the ironized comfort of the group's consensus and simultaneously sense, for the first time, that the ground is shifting. The local details — the silence of the townspeople, the too-legitimate publications, the unexplained specificity of the legend — should begin functioning as O'Connor's offstage gunshots: evidence of a reality the foreground conversation is working very hard not to acknowledge.

---

## Beat 4: Entry Into the Clinic — The Apparatus Revealed

**Concrete Action:** The team enters the abandoned fertility clinic. This is the set piece. Through found footage, first-person camera angles, and Mara's narration, render the space in concrete sensory detail: hallways, examination rooms, filing cabinets, and then — the back greenhouse wing with rows of soil-filled incubators and a functioning grow light. The grow light is the irreducible anomaly. The building has been abandoned for over a decade. There is no active electrical service. The light is on. The team cycles through rational explanations (solar battery, timer, squatters) and each explanation collapses under scrutiny. The documents they find — Gundersen's notes, charts, photographs — are too detailed, too clinically rigorous, too *possible* to dismiss. No one says what they are beginning to think.

**Structural Function — The Accident Scene: Comedy Machinery Becomes Horror Machinery:** This is the car flipping into the ditch. Every element from the comic first half must begin revealing its second function. Mara's cheerful omniscient narration, which was funny when it exposed petty insecurities, becomes horrifying when it exposes *genuine terror that people are hiding behind professional composure.* The found-footage format, which was a gimmick, becomes the only perceptual lens available — the reader, like the characters, can only see what the cameras see, and the cameras keep *not quite capturing* things in the periphery. The team's scientific expertise, which was played for credential comedy, becomes the very apparatus that prevents them from dismissing what they're finding, because *they know enough to know this shouldn't work but can't prove it doesn't.*

**Key Craft Problem to Solve:** The grow light is the story's fulcrum and must be handled with extreme care. It cannot be explained. It also cannot be presented as straightforwardly supernatural — not yet. It must sit in the uncanny valley between malfunction and miracle, forcing both the characters and the reader into an epistemological crisis that mirrors the Abilene Paradox in structure: everyone is disturbed, no one will say so, and the collective performance of calm makes the disturbance worse. The physical environment must be rendered with enough concrete specificity (smells, textures, temperatures, the quality of the light) that the reader's body responds even as the reader's intellect resists.

**What Must Land:** The moment of recognition — analogous to the grandmother's face going white when she realizes the house is in Tennessee — should be the instant a team member reaches for a rational explanation and *hears it ring false in their own mouth.* The reader should feel the genre shift not as a tonal announcement but as a slow, sickening realization that every joke in the first half was a load-bearing structural element aimed at *this room, this light, this silence.* The comedy didn't stop. The comedy was always about this.

---

## Beat 5: The Pumpkins Are Warm — The Irreducible Encounter

**Concrete Action:** Someone touches one of the pumpkins in the incubators. It is warm. Not room temperature. Not sun-warmed from the grow light. Warm the way skin is warm. Warm in a way that implies *metabolism.* The team fragments. Someone wants to leave immediately. Someone wants to take samples. Someone is crying. Someone is recording everything with manic, dissociative professionalism. Mara's narration, for the first time, fails to maintain its cheerful omniscience — it stutters, qualifies, loses its comic timing. The found footage becomes chaotic, multiple cameras running, arguments overlapping. In the text chains afterward, reconstructed in the dossier, the team members' voices are different. The performing is over.

**Structural Function — The Misfit Arrives: The Premise Stops Being a Joke:** This is the moment where the story's satirical premise turns and faces the reader with dead-serious eyes. Like The Misfit stepping out of the hearse-like car, the warm pumpkins are the *literalization of the thing everyone agreed to treat as metaphor.* The Abilene Paradox collapses, but not in the direction anyone expected — it doesn't collapse into shared relief ("we all knew it was fake"), it collapses into shared horror ("it was never fake and none of us are equipped for this"). Mara's narration losing its composure is the structural equivalent of the grandmother's failed rhetorical strategies — the frame that organized reality is breaking down.

**Key Craft Problem to Solve:** The warmth must be conveyed through the document layers, not despite them. A video diary recorded in a shaking hand. A text message that is just: *"it's warm mara. it's warm. what the fuck."* A peer-review comment on Gundersen's old paper, left at 3 AM by a team member who went back to the motel and re-read it, that simply says: *"Methods section holds. I've checked four times. Methods section holds."* The horror is not that science failed — the horror is that science *worked*, that someone actually did this, and the team is qualified enough to recognize it. The format should fracture here the way reality is fracturing for the characters.

**What Must Land:** Like O'Connor's offstage gunshots, the full implications of the warm pumpkins should be felt rather than stated. No one should say "there's a baby in there." The word "baby" should become conspicuous by its absence — a hole in every conversation, the thing every document talks around. The reader should fill in the silence themselves, which makes it worse.

---

## Beat 6: The Vigil — Confronting What Cannot Be Debunked

**Concrete Action:** The team, unable to leave and unable to fully commit to believing, enters a liminal period — hours or a night spent in or near the clinic, monitoring the incubators, arguing, recording, confessing. This is the theological conversation scene. Except the disputation is not about Jesus — it is about the boundaries of biological possibility, the ethics of intervention, and what they owe a living thing that *should not exist.* Someone argues they must open an incubator. Someone argues that doing so might kill whatever is inside. Someone argues that "whatever is inside" is a phrase they should be ashamed of, because they all know what is inside. Mara, privately, in a video diary, confronts her own role: she assembled this team as a career stunt. If something is alive in there, she put it in front of seven people who are too compromised by ambition and denial to respond humanely.

**Structural Function — The Ideas Scene: Theme Dramatized Under Pressure:** O'Connor gives the theological argument to the murderer and strips it from the churchgoer. The structural equivalent here: the most profound ethical clarity should come from the *least credentialed* or most disgraced team member — possibly Mara herself, the veterinary dentist turned journalist whom the specialists have been condescending to all story. The "experts" should be paralyzed by exactlythe expertise that was supposed to make them authoritative. They know too much to act. The person who knows the least about human reproduction but the most about *caring for something alive and vulnerable* might be the one who sees clearly. The Misfit's line — "Jesus thrown everything off balance" — finds its echo in whoever says the thing that reframes the entire story: something like *"It doesn't matter how it got here. It's warm. What are we going to do?"*

**Key Craft Problem to Solve:** This is the scene most at risk of becoming a static debate. It must be dramatized through the document layers — arguments happening simultaneously across video, text, and in-person confrontation, fragmenting and overlapping, with Mara's narration trying and failing to synthesize them into a coherent account. The peer-review comments, which were comic marginalia earlier, could become the most emotionally raw documents here: scientists annotating their own prior certainties and watching them dissolve in real time. The formal gimmick must earn its keep in this beat or it was never worth using.

# The Gundersen Protocol

## A Partial Reconstruction from the Dossier Compiled by the Saskatchewan Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Tisdale Detachment, File No. 2024-TIS-00783

*Introductory note: The following materials were recovered from a 2019 Ford Transit van (Alberta plate CKR-4417) found idling with its headlights on in the parking lot of the Flett Springs Fertility and Agricultural Research Clinic, 11 km northeast of Gronlid, Saskatchewan, on the morning of November 3, 2024. The van's engine had run out of fuel. Seven personal devices, three professional-grade video cameras, one drone (damaged), and a laptop containing an in-progress documentary edit were recovered from the vehicle and from the clinic interior. Eight persons associated with the vehicle remain missing. What follows is an edited reconstruction of materials from those devices, organized as closely to chronological order as the available metadata allows. Ellipses indicate corrupted or irrecoverable data. Bracketed notes are from Constable Dwight Fenn, RCMP, who compiled the file.*

---

# PART ONE

## 1.

**FROM THE LAPTOP — DOCUMENTARY ROUGH CUT, "THE GUNDERSEN PROTOCOL," EDITED BY MARA SHIN**

**[Title card: white text on black]**

THE GUNDERSEN PROTOCOL
*A Documentary by Mara Shin*

**[Title card fades. New text:]**

In 2011, a fertility clinic in rural Saskatchewan closed under unremarkable circumstances. Its director, a Norwegian-born reproductive endocrinologist named Arne Gundersen, surrendered his medical license as part of a settlement with Health Canada. The specific complaints were sealed. The clinic was shuttered. The building was not demolished.

Within two years, the residents of Gronlid (pop. 203) and the surrounding rural municipality of Flett Springs had constructed a legend around the clinic and its final experiments. The story, as it appeared in a 2014 Saskatoon StarPhoenix human-interest column, a 2016 thread on r/UnresolvedMysteries, and a 2019 segment of a podcast called *Morbid Adjacencies* (downloaded 311 times before the feed went dead), goes like this:

Dr. Gundersen believed a human embryo could be gestated to viability inside a living cucurbit — a pumpkin — using a proprietary nutrient-transfer protocol that replaced the function of a human placenta with the vascular system of the fruit. He built a greenhouse wing onto the back of his clinic. He ran trials. He was shut down before any trial reached term.

But the grow lights in the greenhouse are still on.

**[Cut to: Mara Shin, mid-thirties, sitting on the edge of a motel bed. The bedspread has a pattern of geese. She is wearing a hoodie that reads WESTERN COLLEGE OF VETERINARY MEDICINE — DENTAL SPECIALIZATION. There is a stain on it that might be coffee or might be older. She speaks directly into a handheld camera, the angle slightly too low, so the viewer sees mostly chin and ceiling.]**

MARA: Okay. Hi. This is — okay, hi. I'm Mara Shin. I am a journalist. Before I was a journalist, I was a veterinary dental technician. Before I was a veterinary dental technician, I was a journalism student who couldn't afford journalism school. Before that, I was a kid who watched a lot of Barbara Walters. None of these things are particularly relevant, except that what I'm about to tell you requires you to know that I am a serious person. I am serious. I went to school. I have a diploma — two diplomas — and I take things seriously.

**[She looks off camera. Looks back.]**

MARA: The pumpkin baby thing. Okay. So.

**[Cut to black. Title card:]**

Mara Shin was fired from the Western College of Veterinary Medicine in 2022 after a disciplinary review found she had been using university film equipment and lab access to produce an unauthorized documentary about bovine fertility fraud in the Alberta feedlot industry. The documentary, titled *Bull*, was 74% complete. It has never been released. She owes the university $11,400 in equipment fees and has been making minimum payments of $50/month.

She first encountered the Gundersen story in March 2024, in a LaQuinta Inn in Swift Current, Saskatchewan, while driving to a freelance gig photographing a canola festival for a regional agriculture magazine that pays $0.12/word.

She has been building a team for seven months.

**[Cut back to Mara on the bed.]**

MARA: I want to be clear about something. I am not a believer. I don't think there are babies in pumpkins. I think there is a *story* about babies in pumpkins, and the story is interesting because of what it reveals about — about rural folklore, and medical mistrust, and the kind of narrative that grows in a community after an institution fails it. That's the documentary. That's what I'm making. It's a documentary about a *story*. Not about a — not about pumpkins.

**[She pauses.]**

MARA: The grow light thing is weird, though.

---

**[Cut to: Mara's narration over a montage of emails and texts, displayed as screen captures with personal identifiers partially redacted — then un-redacted, because, as Mara's voiceover notes, "I tried to be ethical about this but honestly everyone's going to know who everyone is, so."]**

MARA (V.O.): Here's the thing about assembling an investigative team for a story nobody takes seriously: you can't recruit believers, because believers will contaminate your methodology. And you can't recruit skeptics, because skeptics won't show up. What you need are people who are skeptical enough to say yes *ironically* and committed enough to keep showing up once the irony wears off.

What you need, basically, are academics between jobs.

---

## 2.

**EMAIL — SENT APRIL 14, 2024, 2:17 AM**

**From:** mara.shin.films@gmail.com
**To:** j.kovacs@ucalgary.ca
**Subject:** Documentary opportunity — reproductive endocrinology expertise needed

Dr. Kovacs,

My name is Mara Shin. I'm an independent documentary filmmaker producing a feature-length investigative piece about the Flett Springs Fertility Clinic and the work of Dr. Arne Gundersen. I'm assembling a small team of scientific consultants to visit the clinic site and evaluate the surviving documentation through a rigorous, evidence-based lens. This is NOT a paranormal investigation. This is a serious examination of fringe reproductive science and its cultural afterlife.

I'm reaching out because your 2019 paper on extrauterine fetal development in animal models ("Ectogenesis Revisited: Toward a Functional Artificial Placenta in Caprine Subjects," *Journal of Reproductive Biotechnology*, vol. 34, no. 2) suggests you have the specific technical background to assess Gundersen's claims. I should mention that the project comes with a modest consulting honorarium of $2,500 — I know that's not much, but it also includes travel, accommodation, and meal expenses, and the planned shoot is only 4 days.

Any interest?

Best,
Mara Shin

**[Constable Fenn's note: Dr. Jozsef Kovacs, age 47, Associate Professor (contract) in the Department of Reproductive Biology, University of Calgary. His contract was not renewed for the 2024–25 academic year. He is among the eight missing persons.]**

---

MARA (V.O.): Kovacs said yes within six hours. He asked zero questions about the honorarium, the schedule, or Gundersen. He asked one question, by reply email at 8:04 AM: "Will the documentary include on-camera interviews?" I said yes. He replied: "Good. How should I list this on my CV — as a consultancy or a media appearance?" I said either. He replied: "Both, then."

Here's what I knew about Jozsef Kovacs that Jozsef Kovacs did not know I knew: his lab had just lost its last remaining grant. His wife had moved out in February. His goat-uterus paper, which he considered his life's work, had been cited exactly twice — both times in the same review article, both times as an example of "promising but underfunded approaches." He was, at the time I contacted him, teaching two sections of undergraduate Human Biology as a sessional instructor at Mount Royal University for $6,200 per section. He could not have turned down a camera pointed at his face if it had been mounted on a rifle.

He was my first yes, and everyone else's reason for saying yes.

---

## 3.

**EMAIL — SENT APRIL 22, 2024, 11:56 PM**

**From:** mara.shin.films@gmail.com
**To:** priya.chandrasekaran@usask.ca
**Subject:** Fwd: Documentary opportunity — botanical/agricultural biology expertise needed

Dr. Chandrasekaran,

[…same pitch, adjusted for recipient's expertise…]

I should mention that Dr. Jozsef Kovacs from U of C has already confirmed his participation.

---

MARA (V.O.): Priya Chandrasekaran. Forty-one. Plant physiologist. University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon — tenured, comfortable, theoretically immune to a pitch like mine. And she was immune to my pitch. What she was not immune to was Jozsef Kovacs.

They'd been on a CIHR review panel together in 2021. Three days in Ottawa. Nothing happened. Everything almost happened. Priya told her best friend, Dr. Nuala Dixon — I'll get to Nuala — that Kovacs had "a face like a half-collapsed cathedral" and that she had thought about him in the shower "not often but geometrically." I don't know what that means. The point is that when I wrote "Dr. Jozsef Kovacs has already confirmed his participation," I was not making a scientific argument. I was making the only argument that has ever worked reliably in the history of human decision-making.

Priya said yes within two days. Her email was four paragraphs long. Three paragraphs were about the fascinating intersection of cucurbit physiology and mammalian nutrient exchange. One paragraph, the shortest, asked if the accommodation was "single rooms or shared."

---

## 4.

**TEXT CHAIN — "PRIYA / NUALA" — APRIL 25, 2024**

**PRIYA:** So I did something possibly unhinged
**NUALA:** Scale of 1-10
**PRIYA:** Signed up for a documentary about a man who grew babies in pumpkins
**NUALA:** That's not a number
**PRIYA:** 7?
**NUALA:** Why
**PRIYA:** For science
**NUALA:** Priya
**PRIYA:** Kovacs is going
**NUALA:** There it is
**PRIYA:** It's not ABOUT that. It's tangentially related to my vascular transport work. Cucurbit xylem architecture is genuinely underexplored as a
**NUALA:** Priya I love you but you just typed "cucurbit xylem architecture" like it was a sentence a person says
**PRIYA:** It IS a sentence a person says. I say it regularly. In my TENURED POSITION
**NUALA:** Is his wife still gone
**PRIYA:** I don't know
**PRIYA:** I didn't look
**PRIYA:** February
**NUALA:** So you looked
**PRIYA:** The documentary is about FOLKLORE, Nuala

---

## 5.

MARA (V.O.): The rest of the team came together over the following two months, each one pulled into orbit by the gravitational field of the person who'd said yes before them. It's a principle I learned not in journalism school but in veterinary dental practice: you can't get a nervous dog onto the examination table by pulling the dog. You get a calm dog onto the table first. The nervous dog follows.

Here's the team. I'll be brief because, honestly, some of these people were more interesting on paper than on camera, and this is going to be a long documentary.

**[Montage of email replies, acceptance messages, and profile photos, each accompanied by Mara's narration:]**

**Dr. Nuala Dixon.** Forty-three. Bioethicist, joint appointment at the University of Alberta and the Haskayne School of Business. She publishes on informed consent in experimental medicine. She said yes because Priya said yes and because Nuala has spent fifteen years writing about fringe clinics from a distance and has, I think, always wanted to stand inside one. She would deny this. She sent me a nineteen-page informed consent document to sign before agreeing to participate, which I signed without reading, which she then cited as an example of exactly the kind of consent failure her work critiques. I like Nuala.

**Dr. Todd Kemper.** Fifty-one. Agricultural engineer, recently retired from the Saskatchewan Ministry of Agriculture. Specialty: controlled-environment greenhouse systems. He knows grow lights. He knows soil incubators. He knows how long a solar battery lasts and how a timer switch works and every other boring explanation for why a light might be on in an abandoned building. Todd said yes because his wife told him he needed a hobby that wasn't watching the Saskatchewan Roughriders lose, and because I described the project as "a few days in the field, fresh air, easy work." He is the only person on the team who has actually been to Gronlid. He went once, in 2009, to inspect a commercial greenhouse operation for a provincial subsidy application. He described the town as "fine." Todd is a man who describes most things as "fine."

**Wei-Lin Tsao.** Thirty-four. Postdoctoral fellow, developmental biology, McGill. Specialty: mammalian embryonic implantation. The youngest and most qualified person on the team, which means he's also the most desperate and the most overworked. He's on his second postdoc. He was rejected from eight tenure-track positions last cycle. His supervisor recently listed herself as first author on their joint paper for the third time. When I pitched him, he listened silently to the entire Gundersen story, and when I finished, his only question was: "Is the $2,500 honorarium taxable?" It was the question of a man who has done the math on his life and found it short. I said it could be structured as a travel reimbursement. He said yes.

**Dr. Helen Park.** Fifty-seven. Clinical psychologist, University of Manitoba. Specialty: mass suggestion, shared delusion, folie à groupe. She is the team's designated skeptic — the person I recruited specifically to explain, for the camera, why a small town might convince itself that an eccentric doctor grew babies in pumpkins. Helen's first email to me said, and I will quote this because it's the kind of sentence I couldn't invent: "I've built my career on the principle that collective belief tells you everything about the believers and nothing about the believed. I'd be delighted to demonstrate this in the field." Helen's research has not been funded since 2021. She has been writing a book titled *The Credulity Machine* for six years. It is eleven hundred pages and has no publisher. She came because she needs a Chapter 12.

**Ruben Torres.** Twenty-nine. Not a doctor of anything. MFA in documentary filmmaking, Concordia. My cameraman. My only crew member. I couldn't afford anyone else, and Ruben couldn't afford to say no, because his student loans are structured in a way that I think might technically qualify as art. He has no opinion about pumpkins, babies, or Saskatchewan. He has a strong opinion about lens flares. He is here

In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door.

Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards.

Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood.
